questions.explain: The chapter says worker-thread exhaustion is a real failure mode: when all workers are busy, new requests queue behind the THREADPOOL wait and the instance stops accepting work even though CPU looks idle.
options: CPU utilization spikes to 100%
The buffer pool is flushed to disk
New requests queue behind the THREADPOOL wait and the instance stops accepting work even though CPU looks idle
Queries automatically switch to snapshot isolation
questions.q: What happens when SQL Server's worker-thread pool is exhausted?

questions.explain: The chapter identifies Page Life Expectancy (PLE) as the health metric for the buffer pool; a collapsing PLE means the working set no longer fits in memory, and no query tuning will fix a memory-bound workload.
options: Buffer cache hit ratio
Page Life Expectancy (PLE)
Lock Pages in Memory
Average latch wait time
questions.q: Which metric does the chapter name as the key health indicator for the buffer pool?

questions.explain: The chapter says a log file grown in tiny increments produces too many tiny VLFs, which slows recovery and replication, so log files should be sized deliberately and grown in large, infrequent chunks.
options: The transaction log cannot be backed up
Page splits increase in the data files
Recovery and replication slow down
The buffer pool hit ratio collapses
questions.q: Why does the chapter advise growing transaction log files in large, infrequent chunks?

questions.explain: The chapter explains that escalation from row to page/table locks after roughly 5,000 locks on one object trades memory for blocking surface, and the fix is batching large modifications in controlled chunks.
options: Too many indexes on the table
Lock escalation after roughly 5,000 locks on one object
Snapshot isolation being disabled
A deadlock victim being chosen
questions.q: A single unbatched UPDATE of 100,000 rows suddenly blocks the entire table instead of just the rows it touches. What mechanism does the chapter say causes this?
